html:
The Chané are an Arawakan-speaking people of the foothills between the Andes and the Gran Chaco, in what is now south-eastern Bolivia and north-western Argentina. The map shows them in 1492.

They were settled farmers of maize, beans and squash, known for their pottery and carved wooden masks. Their language belonged to the Arawakan family, which spread far across lowland South America.

From about the 1400s Guaraní-speaking migrants from the east, later called Chiriguanos, moved into these valleys. They conquered many Chané villages, married into them and absorbed them, and most Chané came to speak Guaraní. The mixed groups raided the eastern frontier of the Inca Empire and later held off the Spanish for three centuries. Chané communities still live in Salta province in Argentina, where masked dances at the arete guasu festival keep their old traditions.
